title: Arancini al burro
subtitle: Sicilian butter-and-mozzarella filled rice balls
excerpt: Arancini al burro are the white Sicilian rice ball: saffron-scented rice moulded around a nugget of mozzarella and butter, breaded, and deep-fried until golden. Where the ragù-filled arancini al ragù are savoury and filling, these are lighter and more delicate. They are the Palermitan version of the arancino.
sourceNotes: Sicilian traditional recipe. Arancini al burro (also called arancine in western Sicily) are a Palermitan specialty. Method drawn from traditional Sicilian street food sources and Anna Del Conte, Gastronomy of Italy (2001).

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unfried and bread fresh before frying. Fry from frozen adding 2 minutes to the time.
recipe.batchNotes: Make double and freeze half unfried.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the rice a day ahead. Shape and bread the next day.

glossaryTerms.definition: Sicilian fried rice ball; the name means 'little orange', referring to its golden colour and roughly spherical shape; arancini al burro are the butter-and-mozzarella filled variety.

content.text: Arancini al burro are saffron rice balls filled with mozzarella and butter. The

gets its colour from saffron stirred into the rice while it cooks; the mozzarella and butter filling melts into a pool inside when fried. These are easier to make than the ragù version because the filling requires no separate cooking.

items.prepNote: drained and cut into 1.5 cm cubes
cut into 12 small cubes, one per arancino

content.text: Cook {{arborio-rice}} of rice in {{stock-vegetable}} of hot stock, risotto-style, adding stock ladle by ladle for 18 minutes until just cooked and dense. Stir in {{saffron}} of steeped saffron, the Parmesan, and 30 g of butter. Taste for salt. Spread on a tray and cool completely. Beat 2 eggs into the cooled rice. Refrigerate for 1 hour.

Take about 60 g of rice per arancino. Press flat in your palm. Place a cube of {{mozzarella}} of mozzarella and a small cube of cold butter in the centre. Shape into a compact ball or oval, making sure the filling is fully enclosed.

Dip each arancino in beaten egg and roll firmly in {{breadcrumbs-dried}} of fine breadcrumbs. Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of vegetable oil to 180°C. Fry 3 to 4 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes until deeply golden. Drain on kitchen paper. Eat immediately.

items.symptom: Arancini fall apart in the oil
items.cause: Rice not chilled long enough, or too loose before adding the egg binder.
items.fix: Chill for the full hour. The rice should be sticky enough to hold under gentle pressure.
Steep for at least 10 minutes in warm water before stirring into the hot rice.

content.text: Arancini are Sicilian street food, sold from market stalls and bars across the island, particularly in Palermo and Catania. The butter version is the Palermitan specialty; the ragù version is more common in Catania. In Sicily, arancini are eaten for breakfast or as a mid-morning snack, not as a starter. The saffron in the rice reflects the island's historical Arab influence: saffron came to Sicily with the Arabs in the 9th century and stayed.
